note: First edition, written from the National Museum of Bermuda, Bermuda National Trust, bermuda-online.org, The Bermudian and dive operator sources. Coordinates are approximate until checked on the ground (approx: true). Access notes change: closed forts reopen, reserves close for nesting. Correct anything you find different. Beaches: lifeguards are seasonal (roughly May to September) at Horseshoe Bay, John Smith's Bay and Clearwater; the south shore has rip currents and, in winter and spring, Portuguese man o' war, so check the beach flags. Tides are on the Weather tab. Street art: the Invader mosaics were added on 22 November 2026 from Royal Gazette and Bernews reports; only ten of the 47 have been named publicly, and their coordinates are approximate.

sites.name: Fort St Catherine
sites.access: Open to visitors, usually weekdays to 5pm; $7 adults, $3 children. Guided tours for groups.
sites.kids: The best one for children: tunnels, ramparts, a drawbridge, the powder magazine and cannons, with St Catherine's Beach next door.
sites.see: Tunnels, the keep, big guns on the ramparts, the beach where the Sea Venture survivors came ashore in 1609.
sites.story: First built in 1614 by Governor Moore on the spot where the Sea Venture survivors landed; the fort you see is mostly Victorian. Charlton Heston played Macbeth on the ramparts in the 1950s.

sites.name: Gates Fort
sites.access: Free, small, at the end of Cut Road overlooking the Town Cut.
sites.kids: Five minutes, a good stop to watch a cruise ship squeeze through the Town Cut.
sites.see: A tiny early fort and the view down the channel every ship into St George's uses.
sites.story: Named for Sir Thomas Gates, the Sea Venture's commander. One of the oldest English fortifications anywhere in the New World.

sites.name: Alexandra Battery
sites.access: Free, open site on Barry Road; the beach below is known for sea glass.
sites.kids: Easy. The sea glass beach is the draw; the gun ports are a bonus.
sites.see: A rifled muzzle loader and the wrought iron Gibraltar shield gun ports, rare survivors.
sites.story: Named for Princess Alexandra, later Queen. Reopened to the public in 1998.

sites.name: Fort George
sites.era: 1612 as Riches Mount; present works 1788 and 1840s
sites.access: Houses the Bermuda Maritime Operations Centre; the grounds and the view are reachable, the inside is not.
sites.kids: A short walk up for the view over the town and harbour.
sites.see: An eight pointed star plan, the keep, drawbridges and an 11 inch gun.
sites.story: Has a 150 foot escape tunnel. The radio room inside is where every ship approaching Bermuda is talked in today.

sites.name: Fort William
sites.era: 1830s to 1853, on the site of Warwick Castle
sites.access: Closed for years; visible from the road above the town.
sites.kids: Look only.
sites.see: The roofed over moat and cavernous rooms, from outside.
sites.story: In 1775 Bermudians stole the gunpowder from the magazine here and shipped it to the American rebels; it was used at Bunker Hill.

sites.name: Fort Albert and Fort Victoria
sites.access: Closed; on Retreat Hill above the St Regis, largely under hotel grounds. Parts are visible from the road.
sites.kids: Look only.
sites.see: A pentagonal moated redoubt (Albert) and rock cut works and moats (Victoria).
sites.story: Fort Victoria was armed with eighteen 32 pounders. An 1877 gunpowder fire here was put out by the Royal Artillery before it reached the magazines.

sites.name: Martello Tower, Ferry Reach
sites.access: In Ferry Point Park, free. Inside open 10am to 2pm weekdays in summer, by appointment through the Parks Department in winter.
sites.kids: Good: a round tower you can walk around, the park has trails, a beach and the old ferry landing.
sites.see: Bermuda's only Martello tower, egg shaped with walls nine to eleven feet thick; Burnt Point Fort's neglected remains nearby.
sites.story: Built to cover Ferry Reach against landings; the ferry it guarded was the main road to St George's before the causeway.

sites.name: Great Head Battery and Park
sites.access: Free park at the eastern tip of St David's, parking available.
sites.kids: Cliff edges, so hold hands; otherwise a fine walk with big views and the guns to climb on.
sites.see: The battery and its guns, 24 acres of cliff top parkland, the easternmost point of the island.
sites.story: Manned through the Second World War and never fired at an enemy. The first landfall for anything crossing from Europe.

sites.name: King's Castle, Castle Island
sites.access: By boat only and not open to the general public; the islands are a nature reserve and an archaeological site. Seen from the water on a Castle Harbour boat trip.
sites.kids: From a boat.
sites.see: The oldest standing English stone fort in the New World, the Captain's House of 1621, Devonshire Redoubt on the island behind.
sites.story: In 1614 the garrison fired two of its three cannonballs at two Spanish ships and they turned away: the only Spanish attack on Bermuda.

sites.name: Southampton Fort, Brangman's Island
sites.access: By boat only, no public landing.
sites.kids: From a boat.
sites.see: A small early fort on its own island at the mouth of Castle Harbour.
sites.story: Armed with guns raised from the wreck of the Warwick, the supply ship that sank in Castle Harbour in the 1619 hurricane.

sites.name: Fort Cunningham, Paget Island
sites.access: Not open; the island is reached by boat and the fort is deteriorating.
sites.kids: No.
sites.see: Massive iron fronted casemates and seven 38 ton guns found in 1991, among the few surviving anywhere.
sites.story: The most heavily armed fort in Bermuda when finished, built to stop an American fleet that never came.

sites.name: Fort Hamilton
sites.access: Free, 9:30am to 5pm, Happy Valley Road, a ten minute walk from Front Street.
sites.kids: Excellent: the moat is a garden, there are tunnels to walk through, ramparts and 18 ton guns, and the view over Hamilton Harbour.
sites.see: Moat gardens, the tunnels, the guns, the harbour from the ramparts. The Bermuda Islands Pipe Band plays here on some winter days.
sites.story: Ordered by the Duke of Wellington, finished after his death, and never fired in anger.

sites.name: Scaur Hill Fort and Park
sites.access: Free, 22 acre park off Somerset Road; buses 7 and 8 stop nearby.
sites.kids: Good: the dry moat to run along, the disappearing guns, trails down to the water on both sides.
sites.see: The moat and ramparts, 64 pounder guns on disappearing carriages, the only known examples, and the view across the Great Sound.
sites.story: Built when Britain feared American retaliation for Bermuda's Confederate blockade running; it cut Somerset Island in two with a ditch from shore to shore.

sites.name: West Whale Bay Battery
sites.era: Victorian, over a buried 17th century fort
sites.access: Free park and beach, parking at the top.
sites.kids: A small beach reached down a path, the battery above it, rock pools; a whole morning.
sites.see: The battery, barracks and magazine, and the beach where humpbacks pass in March and April.
sites.story: Guarded the Hog Fish Channel, the western way through the reef. The original 1600s fort lies under the sand.

sites.name: Devonshire Bay Battery
sites.access: Free park, open for sightseeing and swimming.
sites.kids: A quiet bay with a small battery to explore.
sites.see: One of the few surviving south shore coastal batteries, with the bay below.
sites.story: One of a chain of small batteries that once ringed the south shore against raiders.

sites.name: Hungry Bay Fort
sites.access: Remains can be seen from the shore; the mangrove bay is a nature reserve.
sites.kids: Look only.
sites.see: Low remains above the mangrove bay.
sites.story: One of the small parish forts that local militia manned; the bay behind it is the island's largest mangrove swamp.

sites.name: Fort Popple
sites.access: Not accessible; ruins on the eastern side of St David's.
sites.kids: No.
sites.see: Ruins.
sites.story: Named for Governor Alured Popple, who moved the guns here from Smith's Fort on Governor's Island.

sites.name: Smith's Fort, Governor's Island
sites.access: A one acre island in St George's Harbour, not publicly accessible.
sites.kids: From the harbour.
sites.see: A ruined early fort.
sites.story: Its first cannon was raised from the wreck of the Sea Venture.

sites.name: Gunpoint battery, Wreck Hill
sites.access: Private land around Wreck Hill; not a public site.
sites.kids: No.
sites.see: Little remains.
sites.story: In 1777 American privateers landed here, spiked the guns and briefly held the west end: the only invasion of Bermuda.

sites.name: Agar's Island magazine
sites.access: Private island, closed to the public; seen from the Hamilton to Dockyard ferry.
sites.kids: From the ferry.
sites.see: The island itself, from the water.
sites.story: Built as a gunpowder magazine for the fleet; in the 1920s it housed Bermuda's first aquarium.

sites.name: Sea Venture (1609)
sites.access: Little remains on the reef off St Catherine's Point; the story is told at Fort St Catherine and the National Museum.
sites.kids: Tell the story on the beach where they landed.
sites.see: The beach and the reef; artefacts at the National Museum in Dockyard.
sites.story: The flagship of the Virginia Company's relief fleet, driven onto the reef by a hurricane. All 150 aboard survived, built two ships from the wreck and the cedar, and sailed on to Jamestown; the island was settled because of it. Shakespeare's The Tempest is thought to draw on the accounts.

sites.name: Warwick (1619)
sites.access: In Castle Harbour, 40 ft; excavated and not a tourist dive.
sites.kids: The finds at the National Museum.
sites.see: At the museum: gunpowder flask caps, lead weights, a miniature cannon, game counters.
sites.story: The supply ship about to leave for Jamestown when a hurricane sank her at anchor. Found by Teddy Tucker and Mendel Peterson in 1967 and excavated 2008 to 2012. Her guns went to Southampton Fort.

sites.name: L'Herminie (1838)
sites.access: Dive, about 35 ft, by boat with a dive operator.
sites.kids: Not snorkelable; the museum pieces are the kids' version.
sites.see: Up to 40 cannon lying on the reef.
sites.story: A French 60 gun frigate diverted to Bermuda in heavy seas and lost on the western reef. Locals salvaged her stores and sold them in town; a sextant, a soup tureen and a gun lock are at the National Museum.

sites.name: Montana (1863)
sites.access: Dive or snorkel, 30 ft, by boat; usually visited with the Constellation beside it.
sites.kids: A good first wreck snorkel with a calm day and an operator.
sites.see: Paddlewheel frames, boilers and furnace, heavily grown with coral.
sites.story: A Confederate blockade runner (also sailed as the Nola) caught in a storm looking for shelter. Her guns and cargo were mostly salvaged at the time.

sites.name: Constellation (1943)
sites.access: Dive or snorkel, 26 to 30 ft, right beside the Montana.
sites.kids: Snorkelable on a calm day with an operator.
sites.see: Cement bags set like stone, thousands of bottles, drug ampoules scattered on the reef.
sites.story: A four masted wooden schooner carrying cargo to Venezuela that struck the reef with all hands saved. Peter Benchley's The Deep was written around her, and the film used the wreck's groaning.

sites.name: Mary Celestia (1864)
sites.access: Dive, 55 to 60 ft, by boat.
sites.kids: No; the perfume story is the kids' version.
sites.see: The intact paddlewheel standing up from the sand, engine, boilers, bow and anchor.
sites.story: A Civil War blockade runner that hit the reef leaving for the Carolinas. After a 2011 hurricane shifted the sand, archaeologists found sealed perfume bottles in the bow; the scent was recreated and is sold in Hamilton.

sites.name: North Carolina (1880)
sites.access: Dive, 25 to 45 ft, by boat; visibility can be poor.
sites.kids: No.
sites.see: An iron hull with triple deadeyes still along the rails, thick with fish.
sites.story: A Liverpool barque that grounded on New Year's Day; the refloating went wrong when her own anchor holed her.

sites.name: HMS Vixen (1896)
sites.access: Snorkel from a boat; her bow breaks the surface, the rest is in 20 to 35 ft.
sites.kids: The best wreck for children: you can see it from the surface.
sites.see: A Victorian ironclad gunboat with the bow out of the water and the hull just below.
sites.story: Sunk on purpose to block the channel at Daniel's Head against torpedo boats. The first wreck on the glass bottom boat route for a century.

sites.name: Pollockshields (1915)
sites.access: Dive, about 40 ft, a short swim out from Elbow Beach on a calm day with an operator.
sites.kids: No; you can point to the spot from the beach.
sites.see: Two boilers, a propeller and the engine.
sites.story: A steamer carrying First World War shells and gunpowder, driven onto the reef in fog and a hurricane. Everyone was rescued but the captain. The police cleared the last live cargo in 1999.

sites.name: King George dredger (1930s)
sites.parish: Off the Town Cut, St George's
sites.access: Dive, 60 ft, sitting upright.
sites.kids: No.
sites.see: Ladders, catwalks, winches, engines and the forward holds, all intact.
sites.story: The government dredger that cut the Town Cut deeper from 1911 so bigger ships could reach St George's, then sunk when it was worn out.

sites.name: Cristobal Colon (1936)
sites.access: Dive or snorkel, 15 to 60 ft, spread over a huge area; by boat.
sites.kids: Snorkelable in parts on a calm day with an operator.
sites.see: Engines, turbines and propellers of a 500 ft liner, Bermuda's largest wreck.
sites.story: A Spanish luxury liner whose captain mistook a radio tower for a lighthouse. Islanders stripped her of furniture and fittings for years; the Americans then used her for bombing practice in the war.

sites.name: Iristo (1937)
sites.access: Dive, 55 ft, bow rising to 18 ft.
sites.kids: No.
sites.see: A split hull, a fire engine and a steamroller she was carrying, boilers and a spare propeller.
sites.story: A Norwegian steamer that hit the reef while steering around the Cristobal Colon, a few months after her, and sank under tow a mile and a half away.

sites.name: Hermes (1984)
sites.access: Dive, 80 ft, by boat; a favourite because it sits upright and intact.
sites.kids: No.
sites.see: A whole ship on the sand, wheelhouse and holds open to swim through.
sites.story: A 1943 US Coast Guard buoy tender turned freighter, abandoned in Bermuda with a dead engine, sold to the dive association for one dollar and sunk as a reef.

sites.name: The Airplane, B-50 (1961)
sites.access: Dive, about 30 ft.
sites.kids: No.
sites.see: Wings, engines and landing gear of a US Air Force bomber.
sites.story: A B-50 that lost power after taking off from Kindley Field and ditched on the north reef; the crew got out.

sites.name: NASA tracking station, Cooper's Island
sites.access: Cooper's Island Nature Reserve, free, trails and beaches; the old station buildings and the radar tower are inside the reserve.
sites.kids: One of the best outings on the island: beaches, trails, the tower, and the story of the moon landing.
sites.see: The tower, the remaining buildings, Clearwater and Turtle Bay beaches, Castle Harbour views, and the small NASA mobile station that returned in 2012.
sites.story: Built for Project Mercury, the station made the Go or No Go call on 118 launches and tracked the Apollo 11 rocket for a quarter of an hour after it left for the moon. Up to 132 people worked here, 50 of them Bermudian.

sites.name: Kindley Field and the US Naval Air Station
sites.access: The airport sits on it; the old base housing, the hospital site and the Southside area are public roads. Clearwater Beach was the base beach.
sites.kids: Southside's beaches and the airport viewing.
sites.see: The scale of the landfill that joined the islands, the base era buildings along Southside, the old hospital site.
sites.story: Built by the United States in 1941 on land leased for 99 years, joining St David's and the islands of Castle Harbour with fill; the Americans left in 1995 and the land came back in 2002. The civilian airport grew out of the base.

sites.name: Daniel's Head, the Canadian station
sites.access: The peninsula is a park; the later resort on the site closed and the cabins are gone. The beaches are open.
sites.kids: Quiet beaches and the Vixen wreck offshore.
sites.see: Foundations and the shoreline the Canadians used for listening to the Atlantic.
sites.story: Canadian Forces Station Daniel's Head listened for Soviet submarines for thirty years. The 9 Beaches resort that followed is gone too, leaving the point to the longtails.

sites.name: Darrell's Island flying boat base
sites.access: By boat only; the island is used by the Bermuda Regiment and others, so landing is not generally open. Seen from the ferry.
sites.kids: From the ferry.
sites.see: The old terminal and slipways from the water.
sites.story: Bermuda's first airport: Imperial Airways and Pan Am flying boats landed on the Great Sound and taxied to Darrell's Island from 1937, and Clippers from New York made the island a weekend trip. It closed when Kindley Field opened to civilian flights.

sites.name: The Bermuda Railway
sites.access: The Railway Trail is a free public path along most of the old line; the Bailey's Bay footbridges reopened in 2017.
sites.kids: Flat, stroller friendly stretches, the bridges over the water at Bailey's Bay, the cuttings and tunnels.
sites.see: Cuttings, bridge piers, the restored trestles at Bailey's Bay, the old station sites, the Railway Museum at Aquarium Road.
sites.story: Twenty two miles of narrow gauge from St George's to Somerset, with 33 bridges and trestles, built for a fortune and sold for scrap to British Guiana after the war. The rails went; the path stayed.

sites.name: Casemate Barracks, Dockyard
sites.access: Within the National Museum of Bermuda grounds at Dockyard; restoration continuing.
sites.kids: Part of a museum day, with the Dolphin Quest lagoon and the ramparts.
sites.see: A massive barrack block built by convicts, the old cells, the ramparts and the Keep.
sites.story: Built by convict labour to house the garrison of the Royal Naval Dockyard, then Bermuda's maximum security prison for thirty years, and now being restored by the museum.

sites.name: Tudor Hill naval station
sites.access: The buildings have had various government and private uses since; not a public site.
sites.kids: No.
sites.see: Cold War buildings on the hill above the south shore.
sites.story: A United States Navy listening post that tracked submarines by sound across the Atlantic; one of the quieter parts of the American presence on the island.

sites.name: Club Med site, St George's
sites.access: The St Regis now stands on the site; Fort St Catherine and the beach next door are public.
sites.kids: Nothing to see of it now; the story only.
sites.see: Nothing of the old hotel remains.
sites.story: For twenty years the empty tower above Fort St Catherine was Bermuda's most famous eyesore, a resort that closed in 1988 and stood derelict until demolition in 2008. The ground under it holds Fort Victoria.

sites.name: Lagoon Park and the pond ruin, Ireland Island South
sites.era: Royal Navy land from 1809; park today
sites.access: Free, sunrise to sunset; cross Grey's Bridge south from Dockyard, or buses 7 and 8 to the cemetery stop.
sites.kids: A favourite: lawns, picnic tables, the lagoon with its birds, trails, and the derelict building by the pond to peer into from outside.
sites.see: The lagoon and its birds, the view down the Great Sound, the ruined building at the pond, Easter lilies in spring, the Royal Naval Cemetery in the next valley.
sites.story: Part of the land the Admiralty bought in 1809 to build the Dockyard; the lagoon and its surroundings served the navy for a century and a half before becoming a park. Matt's note: the building at the pond is one of the island's better abandoned ones. Its history is still to be pinned down.

sites.name: Glass Beach (Black Bay), Ireland Island South
sites.access: Free. On the north side of Malabar Road opposite the Royal Naval Cemetery; walk down from the cemetery bus stop. Best at low tide; the small beaches all but vanish at high tide.
sites.kids: Sea glass hunting, shallow water, a short walk. Check the tide on the Weather tab first.
sites.see: A beach made of a century of the navy's bottles, worn smooth; the Great Sound; the cemetery across the road.
sites.story: Generations of Dockyard rubbish went over the edge here, and the sea has been polishing it ever since. Take photos, not glass, if you want it to stay a glass beach.

sites.name: Royal Naval Cemetery (The Glade)
sites.access: Free, dawn to dusk, on Malabar Road between Malabar and Craddock Roads near Parson's Bay; buses 7 and 8 stop at it.
sites.kids: A quiet walk among old stones; the Oration Stand is the thing to find.
sites.see: About 866 graves over 2.73 acres, the Oration Stand where funeral speeches were given, and the oldest legible stone, Sergeant John Kitchener of the Royal Marines, 1816.
sites.story: The navy's own burial ground from the founding of the Dockyard, filled in the yellow fever years when ships lost whole crews. From 1853 only Ireland Island residents and navy people could be buried here.
links: Bermuda National Trust, cemeteries of the west

sites.name: Convict Cemetery, Ireland Island
sites.access: Free, dawn to dusk; hidden at the west end of Cochrane Road, off Malabar Road.
sites.kids: Short, and a hard story told simply: the men who built the forts.
sites.see: Thirteen visible graves in a small walled plot.
sites.story: From 1824 Britain shipped about 9,000 convicts to Bermuda to build the Dockyard and the forts, housed in prison hulks moored off Ireland Island. Around 2,000 of them died here, of yellow fever and the work; these thirteen stones are what remains of their burial ground.
links: Bermuda National Trust, cemeteries of the west

sites.name: Horseshoe Bay
sites.access: Free; large car park, loos, showers, a cafe and rentals in season, lifeguards in summer. Busy on cruise days.
sites.kids: The famous one, and it earns it: pink sand, a wide shallow edge, and Port Royal Cove (Baby Beach) at the east end, a sheltered pool that is perfect for toddlers.
sites.see: Pink sand, the rock arches, the trail along the dunes to Chaplin and Stonehole Bays.
sites.story: Lifeguarded, which matters on the south shore: the surf and the rip can be strong. Go early or late on a cruise day.

sites.name: Port Royal Cove (Baby Beach)
sites.access: Free; the sheltered cove at the eastern end of Horseshoe Bay, same car park.
sites.kids: The best toddler beach on the island: knee deep, enclosed by rocks, no surf.
sites.see: Rock pools, tiny fish, the view back along Horseshoe.
sites.story: Known to every local parent as Baby Beach.

sites.name: Warwick Long Bay
sites.access: Free; car park off South Road, no facilities beyond a loo in season.
sites.kids: Half a mile of sand and usually nearly empty; the surf can be bigger than Horseshoe, so stay by the edge with little ones.
sites.see: The longest beach on the island, the offshore rock, the dune trail west to Jobson's Cove.
sites.story: Part of South Shore Park, the string of beaches from here to Horseshoe joined by trails over the dunes.

sites.name: Jobson's Cove
sites.access: Free; park at Warwick Long Bay and walk five minutes west along the trail.
sites.kids: A tiny cove almost fully enclosed by rock: calm, shallow, and the most photographed swimming hole in Bermuda. Gets crowded by late morning.
sites.see: Cliffs on three sides, clear water, rock pools at the edges.
sites.story: The cove is a collapsed cave; the rocks around it are the island's limestone at its most sculptural.

sites.name: Stonehole Bay and Chaplin Bay
sites.access: Free; on the dune trail between Jobson's Cove and Horseshoe Bay, no facilities.
sites.kids: Two small beaches with sand and rock, quieter than their neighbours; Chaplin has a natural arch.
sites.see: The rock formations, the arch at Chaplin Bay, longtails nesting in the cliffs in spring.
sites.story: The quiet middle of South Shore Park.

sites.name: Astwood Cove and Park
sites.access: Free; car park at Astwood Park on South Road, steps down to the beach.
sites.kids: A grassy cliff top park for a picnic, a steep path down to a small beach; better for a walk than a long swim with a toddler.
sites.see: Longtails in the cliffs (spring), the park's cedars, the view along the south shore.
sites.story: A favourite wedding spot and one of the best places to watch longtails close up.

sites.name: Elbow Beach (public end)
sites.access: Free at the public western end off Tribe Road 4; the hotel section is for guests. No facilities on the public part.
sites.kids: Good sand, moderate surf, a long walk along the water; the reef close in means snorkelling for older kids.
sites.see: The reef just off the beach, the wreck of the Pollockshields beyond it, the hotel's long beach to the east.
sites.story: The Pollockshields struck the reef here in 1915 with a hold full of ammunition.

sites.name: Grape Bay
sites.access: Free; a small beach reached by a lane off Grape Bay Drive, limited parking.
sites.kids: Quiet and residential, decent sand, little shade; for a quick swim rather than a day.
sites.see: A calm south shore beach on a settled day.
sites.story: One of the parish beaches locals use when the big ones are busy.

sites.name: Marley Beach
sites.access: Free; off South Road by Marley Beach Cottages, parking tight, a path down.
sites.kids: Sheltered by reef, often calm, a good family beach that visitors miss.
sites.see: Rock pools at the ends, the reef, the cottages above.
sites.story: Quiet because the parking is hard; worth it.

sites.name: Church Bay
sites.access: Free; small car park on South Road, steps down, loo at the top.
sites.kids: The best easy snorkelling on the island for older children: the reef starts a few metres out. Not much beach at high tide, so check the tide.
sites.see: Parrotfish and sergeant majors on the reef, the small park above with picnic tables.
sites.story: Named for the church on the hill; the reef is part of the south shore boiler reefs.

sites.name: West Whale Bay
sites.access: Free; park at the top by the battery, a path down. No facilities.
sites.kids: Small, sheltered, with rock pools; combine with the battery above.
sites.see: The old battery, the pools, humpbacks offshore in March and April.
sites.story: See the Forts entry for the battery; this is the beach it guarded.

sites.name: Somerset Long Bay
sites.access: Free; park and playground, loos, picnic tables, a nature reserve and pond behind.
sites.kids: One of the best for small children: long, shallow, calm, with a playground and lawn for the non swimmers.
sites.see: The pond with its birds (Audubon reserve), the long shallow bay, sunsets.
sites.story: On the Great Sound side, so sheltered from the south shore swell.

sites.name: Daniel's Head
sites.access: Free; the park on the point beyond Somerset Long Bay, parking by the road.
sites.kids: Shallow sandy coves facing the Sound, quiet, with the Vixen wreck's bow visible offshore.
sites.see: The wreck, the coves, the old base foundations.
sites.story: The Canadian station's beaches; see the Explore ruins entry.

sites.name: Snorkel Park, Dockyard
sites.access: Paid entry; rentals, cafe, bar, lifeguards; next to the ferry and cruise terminal.
sites.kids: Easy and organised for a day with kids, with everything on hand; crowded on cruise days.
sites.see: Calm water inside the Dockyard breakwater, snorkelling gear and pedal boats for hire.
sites.story: Built on the old naval dockyard's beach; a convenient one for ferry days.

sites.name: Mangrove Bay
sites.access: Free; the public bay in Somerset Village, small beach, shops and food nearby.
sites.kids: Shallow and calm, easy to reach with a stroller, ice cream a minute away.
sites.see: The village, the old boats, the bay.
sites.story: The heart of Somerset Village; the regatta runs here in summer.

sites.name: Glass Beach (Black Bay)
sites.access: Free; opposite the Royal Naval Cemetery on Malabar Road. Best at low tide.
sites.kids: Sea glass hunting more than swimming; shallow when the tide is out.
sites.see: Sea glass, the Sound.
sites.story: See the Explore ruins entry.

sites.name: Shelly Bay
sites.access: Free; big car park, playground, loo, a cafe in season, a lawn and a nature reserve behind.
sites.kids: The locals' toddler beach on the north shore: shallow for a long way out, warm, calm, with the playground beside it.
sites.see: The playground, the long shallows, the Railway Trail from here to Bailey's Bay.
sites.story: Named for one of the first settlers; the bay's shallows are why every parent on the island knows it.

sites.name: Clearwater Beach and Turtle Bay
sites.access: Free; car park, loos, a cafe in season, lifeguards in summer, inside Cooper's Island reserve.
sites.kids: Two of the best family beaches on the island, sandy and sheltered, with the Cooper's Island trails and the NASA tower to explore after.
sites.see: Turtle Bay's shallows, the trails to the point, the tower.
sites.story: The old base's beach; see the NASA entry.

sites.name: John Smith's Bay
sites.access: Free; parking on the road, loo, lifeguards in summer, a lunch wagon most days.
sites.kids: A good south shore beach with lifeguards, usually calmer than Horseshoe; the reef is close enough for snorkelling.
sites.see: The reef, the headlands, Spittal Pond next door for a walk.
sites.story: The parish beach of Smith's; combine with Spittal Pond.

sites.name: Devonshire Bay
sites.access: Free; a small bay with a battery and park, parking by the road.
sites.kids: Sheltered and small, with the old battery to explore.
sites.see: The battery, the fishing boats, the bay.
sites.story: See the Forts entry.

sites.name: Tobacco Bay
sites.access: Free entry; rentals, a bar and food, loos, music at weekends in summer; a short walk from Fort St Catherine.
sites.kids: Shallow water inside the rocks and excellent snorkelling for older kids right off the beach; busy in summer.
sites.see: The limestone pillars, fish in the shallows, the fort around the corner.
sites.story: Where the stolen gunpowder of 1775 was rowed out to the American ships.

sites.name: Achilles Bay
sites.access: Free; between Tobacco Bay and Fort St Catherine, small, a beach cafe in season.
sites.kids: Small and sheltered, less busy than Tobacco Bay.
sites.see: The fort above, the rocks.
sites.story: The quieter neighbour.

sites.name: St Catherine's Beach
sites.access: Free; below Fort St Catherine, parking at the fort.
sites.kids: Sandy, calm most days, with the fort to visit after.
sites.see: The fort, the point where the Sea Venture survivors came ashore.
sites.story: See the fort and the Sea Venture entries.

sites.name: Whalebone Bay, Ferry Reach
sites.access: Free; in Ferry Point Park near the Martello Tower.
sites.kids: A small sheltered beach on the Reach, quiet, with the park trails and the tower.
sites.see: The Martello Tower, the old ferry landing, the Railway Trail.
sites.story: See the Martello Tower entry.

sites.name: Clarence Cove, Admiralty House Park
sites.access: Free; park off Spanish Point Road, steps down, caves and cliff jumping for the brave.
sites.kids: A small cove with calm water and caves in the cliffs; older kids love it, keep little ones away from the jumping rocks.
sites.see: The caves cut by the navy, the cliffs, the park's lawns above.
sites.story: The Admiralty's house once stood in the park; the caves were cut for the fleet's stores.

sites.name: Spanish Point Park
sites.access: Free; small beaches and a park at the tip of the point, parking by the road.
sites.kids: Shallow, calm, small; a picnic spot with a view of Dockyard across the water.
sites.see: The wreck of a floating dock offshore, sunsets over the Sound.
sites.story: The floating dock HMS Bermuda was wrecked here in 1902 and its remains still show.

sites.name: Hog Bay Park
sites.access: Free; a 32 acre park with a walk of about 20 minutes down to the shore; the beach only appears at low tide.
sites.kids: A proper little expedition: fields, trails, and a beach that is there or not depending on the tide. Check the Weather tab's tides first.
sites.see: Farm fields, the old boiler reefs, a sunset beach when the tide is right.
sites.story: Bermuda's largest park on the west end.

sites.name: Long Bay, St David's
sites.access: Free; at Southside, below the old base housing, parking by the road.
sites.kids: Quiet sand on the south side of St David's, a locals' beach.
sites.see: The reef, the views toward Castle Harbour.
sites.story: Part of the Southside area returned from the US base.

sites.name: The Invader mosaic hunt
sites.access: Free. 47 mosaics at 44 spots island wide, on walls, bridges, bus shelters and landmarks. Some are on private property, so look from the road or the path.
sites.kids: A treasure hunt across the whole island. The artist's free Flash Invaders app scores each one you photograph.
sites.see: Small tile pictures in the blocky style of early video games, some easy to spot and some tucked away on purpose.
sites.story: French street artist Invader has been putting pixel mosaics on city walls since 1998. In November 2026 he finished his first invasion of a whole country here, with 47 pieces in all nine parishes, arranged with the Hamilton Princess, the Government and the property owners. No full list of the spots has been published, which is the point: you find them. The ten the newspapers have named are listed here.

sites.name: Invader mosaic at Ice Queen
sites.access: Free; on the Ice Queen restaurant at Rural Hill Plaza, South Road. Parking in the plaza.
sites.kids: An easy one to start with, and there is ice cream.
sites.see: A pixel Homer Simpson.
sites.story: One of 47 pixel mosaics the French street artist Invader put up across all nine parishes in November 2026, his first invasion of a whole country. Each one is made of small tiles in the style of early video games.

sites.name: Invader mosaic at the Boaz Island bus shelter
sites.access: Free; on the bus shelter at Boaz Island on the road to Dockyard, buses 7 and 8.
sites.kids: Spot it from the bus on the way to Dockyard.
sites.see: A pixel Papa Smurf, nicknamed Smurf's Up.
sites.story: One of 47 pixel mosaics the French street artist Invader put up across all nine parishes in November 2026, his first invasion of a whole country. Each one is made of small tiles in the style of early video games.

sites.name: Invader mosaic at Somerset Bridge
sites.access: Free; at Somerset Bridge on Somerset Road. Park nearby and walk; the road is narrow.
sites.kids: Pair it with the world's smallest drawbridge.
sites.see: A pixel mosaic by the bridge.
sites.story: One of 47 pixel mosaics the French street artist Invader put up across all nine parishes in November 2026, his first invasion of a whole country. Each one is made of small tiles in the style of early video games.

sites.name: Invader mosaic at Port Royal Gas Station

sites.kids: Look while you fill up.
sites.see: A tiled pixel piece on the station building.
sites.story: One of 47 pixel mosaics the French street artist Invader put up across all nine parishes in November 2026, his first invasion of a whole country. Each one is made of small tiles in the style of early video games.

sites.name: Invader mosaic at Southlands
sites.access: Free; on a wall at Southlands beach, in Southlands Park off South Road. A short walk down from the road.
sites.kids: A walk through the park to the beach, with a mosaic to find at the end.

sites.story: One of 47 pixel mosaics the French street artist Invader put up across all nine parishes in November 2026, his first invasion of a whole country. Each one is made of small tiles in the style of early video games.

sites.name: Invader mosaic on the Hamilton Princess moongate
sites.access: Free; on a moongate at the Hamilton Princess & Beach Club, Pitts Bay Road. The hotel grounds are open to visitors.
sites.kids: The hotel helped bring the project to Bermuda, and its art collection is worth a walk through.
